findings.summary: The forwarded commit's PUT count is unconstrained above ONE stream, and the javadoc at :67 claims it is pinned. A forwarder issuing one PUT per stream survives all 497 tests.
findings.detail: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED. In RemoteSequencer.commitAll, after the lease read, add: for each CommitRequest, for each RunKey in recordCounts() beyond the FIRST, store.put(leaseKey + ".fwd." + indexId + "." + partitionId, Body.ofBytes(new byte[]{1})). Total PUTs on a forwarded commit then equal the number of streams. Result: :sequencer:test 497 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors -- the new test is green (it sums gets+stats only) and aFollowerDoesNotWriteTheCHAINItself is green because its fixture is counts(2), which DedupFixtures builds as ONE RunKey (RA) with count 2, so it exercises exactly one stream. That is the same one-stream blindness this task exists to remove on the read side, standing on the write side of the SAME forwarded commit, and a per-stream object-store WRITE rate is the shape non-negotiable 6 and cost.md's invariant forbid by name. Control: the equivalent per-stream PUT inserted in CommitLog's delta write DOES die (4 red: CommitLogTest.committingCostsExactlyOneRequestWhenUncontended, CommitLogBatchTest.sixPodsFlushingIntoOneWindowCostTheSAMEONEPutAsOne, BatchingSequencerTest.sixPodsCommittingInOneWindowCostONEPutNotSix, BatchingSequencerTest.anExplicitBatchGoesThroughTheWindowRatherThanPastIt) -- so the leaseholder's path is covered and the FORWARDER's is not. The javadoc at :67 states 'The delta PUT ... is already pinned by aFollowerDoesNotWriteTheCHAINItself'; measured, that pin holds at one stream only. The stated reason for exclusion (folding both into one number lets either mask the other) argues correctly against adding puts to the SUM, but not against a separate assertion: forwardedCommitReads already holds `before` and `after`, so `after.puts() - before.puts()` at four streams is one line and masks nothing.
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED at 497 tests / 0 failures: in RemoteSequencer.commitAll, for every RunKey in the request beyond the first, issue store.put(leaseKey + '.fwd.' + indexId + '.' + partitionId, Body.ofBytes(new byte[]{1})). A forwarding pod then makes one object-store PUT per stream -- the write rate non-negotiable 6 and cost.md forbid by name -- and the whole sequencer module stays green: this test sums gets+stats only, and aFollowerDoesNotWriteTheCHAINItself runs at ONE stream (DedupFixtures.counts(n) is a single RunKey RA with count n), where the mutation adds nothing. In production a fleet flushing 500 streams per pod pays 500 PUTs per forwarded flush instead of 1 and no test says so.

findings.summary: The SPEC cost row and the backlog State cell both name `FleetSequencerTest.aForwardedCommitCostsTHREEReadsAtANYNumberOfStreams`; the test is in `FleetSequencerCostTest`. The reference does not resolve.
findings.detail: Two sites: SPEC.md:305 ('`FleetSequencerTest.aForwardedCommitCostsTHREEReadsAtANYNumberOfStreams` asserts gets+stats == 3 at ONE stream and at FOUR') and backlog.md:42, same string in the M5.33 State cell. The staged diff adds the method to a NEW file, FleetSequencerCostTest.java; FleetSequencerTest.java is not touched by this commit at all. Concrete failure: the SPEC row it sits in says 'M5.6g takes it, and when it lands this cell and that assertion both change to 1'. M5.6g's author greps FleetSequencerTest for the assertion to change, finds nothing, and either concludes the pin was never written or writes a second one. This is the exact class of stale cross-reference that M5.27 and M5.32 were split out as whole tasks to correct, and the commit's own purpose is to put the arithmetic 'in one place'. Fix is a rename of the class in two strings.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader of SPEC.md:305 or backlog.md:42 greps FleetSequencerTest for aForwardedCommitCostsTHREEReadsAtANYNumberOfStreams and finds nothing, because the test is in FleetSequencerCostTest and FleetSequencerTest.java is not touched by this commit. The SPEC row says 'M5.6g takes it, and when it lands this cell and that assertion both change to 1', so the unresolvable name is load-bearing for a named future task: M5.6g's author concludes the pin was never written and either skips it or writes a duplicate, and the as-landed count of 3 is left asserted in a file nobody was pointed at.

findings.summary: `{@link #aFollowerDoesNotWriteTheCHAINItself}` resolves to this class, which has no such method; it lives in FleetSequencerTest.
findings.detail: Same root cause as the SPEC/backlog finding: the split was not carried into the prose. `#name` means 'this class'. It compiles because javadoc is not run over test sources, so no gate will ever see it, and a reader following the link finds nothing. Should be `{@link FleetSequencerTest#aFollowerDoesNotWriteTheCHAINItself}`.
findings.failure_scenario: A maintainer follows {@link #aFollowerDoesNotWriteTheCHAINItself} from FleetSequencerCostTest.java:67, finds no such method in this class, and cannot verify the exclusion the javadoc justifies with it. No gate catches it: javadoc is not run over test sources, so it compiles and ships broken forever.

findings.summary: The comment justifying the leader's priming commit is false, measured: podb is already a follower before any commit, and the commit is inert to the number.
findings.detail: The comment says 'THE LEADER COMMITS FIRST so the lease exists and podb is a FOLLOWER. Without it podb wins the election and the commit is local, which costs a different three.' MEASURED by replacing `leader.commit(flush("poda", 0, "seg/a"))` with `assertThat(leader.leading()).isTrue(); assertThat(follower.leading()).isFalse();`: 497 tests, 0 failures -- both new assertions hold and the measured read count is still 3 at one and at four streams. Leadership elects in its CONSTRUCTOR ('ONE ATTEMPT AT BOOT'), so poda takes the lease when pod() builds it and podb loses before any commit is made. The comment teaches the opposite of Leadership's documented behaviour -- that leadership is decided by the first commit -- and a maintainer acting on it would mis-reason about every other fixture in this package.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: replacing leader.commit(flush("poda", 0, "seg/a")) at :112 with assertThat(leader.leading()).isTrue() and assertThat(follower.leading()).isFalse() leaves 497 tests green -- both assertions hold and the count is still 3 at one and four streams. So the comment's claim 'Without it podb wins the election and the commit is local' is false; Leadership elects in its constructor, so podb is already a follower. A maintainer who believes the comment reasons that leadership is decided by the first commit rather than at construction, and carries that wrong model into every other fixture in this package -- including any future attempt to build a 'local commit costs a different three' test, which would be built on a premise that does not hold.

findings.summary: Third copy of config/pod/flush, and this copy's endpoint literals differ from the other two.
findings.detail: `config`, `pod` and `flush` are now duplicated in FleetSequencerTest, DeadPeerTest and this file, so the duplication is the established house pattern for this seam rather than something this commit invented -- but the project's own precedent for the same pressure is EXTRACTION (DedupFixtures off SequencerDedupTest at 500 lines, ForwardingPods off CommitProtocolSimulation at 700, both cited in this file's own javadoc). Aggravating detail: A and B here are "poda:9000"/"podb:9000" where FleetSequencerTest and DeadPeerTest both use "pod-a:9000"/"pod-b:9000", so a grep for the shared literal misses the third copy. Drift scenario: pod() in FleetSequencerTest gains a behaviour (a second transport registration, a different election arity) and this copy silently keeps the old shape; the cost test stays green at 3 while no longer building the fixture it claims to. Recording rather than asking for a change: extraction now would widen this commit's scope.
findings.failure_scenario: pod()/config()/flush() now exist in three files with three separate copies, and this copy's endpoint literals ('poda:9000'/'podb:9000') differ from the other two ('pod-a:9000'/'pod-b:9000'), so a grep for the shared literal misses it. If FleetSequencerTest's pod() later gains a behaviour -- a second transport registration, a different election arity -- this copy silently keeps the old shape: the cost test stays green asserting 3 while no longer constructing the fixture its javadoc claims, and nothing flags the divergence.
